chapters.title: Securite, Mayday Repetition And Safety Escalation Sequences

sections.title: The examples below cover exact wording for SECURITE safety b
sections.text: The examples below cover exact wording for SECURITE safety broadcasts, for repeating a MAYDAY call and reporting position on request, and for how a real situation escalates step by step from a safety notice through urgency to full distress. Knowing the exact call structure for each level, and when to move from one level to the next, is as important as knowing the individual prowords in isolation.

sections.title: Responding To A SECURITE Message About A SAR Area
sections.text: On hearing a SECURITE broadcast asking vessels to keep clear of a search-and-rescue area, note the position and extent of the area, plot it on the chart, and adjust the passage plan to stay well clear, typically at least two nautical miles unless the message states otherwise. Reduce speed, post an extra lookout, and if the new track will pass close regardless, call the station that issued the SECURITE to confirm safe passage: "MRCC, MRCC, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, REQUESTING CONFIRMATION SAFE TO PASS TWO MILES SOUTH OF THE REPORTED SAR AREA, OVER."

sections.title: Diverting Course After A SECURITE Hazard Warning
sections.text: On receiving a SECURITE warning about a hazard in your planned route, such as a drifting container, plot the hazard's reported position on the chart, calculate a safe passing distance of at least two nautical miles, plan the new course, and inform the crew before altering course. No special proword is needed to acknowledge a SECURITE broadcast unless a direct reply is required; the appropriate response is usually simply to act on the information and to log it.

sections.title: Sending A SECURITE Safety Broadcast
sections.text: To send your own safety broadcast, first send the announcement on Channel 16: "SECURITE, SECURITE, SECURITE, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS COASTAL GUARDIAN, COASTAL GUARDIAN, COASTAL GUARDIAN, LISTEN ON CHANNEL SIX-SEVEN FOR A SAFETY MESSAGE, OUT." Then switch to the announced working channel and give the actual safety information, for example a drifting hazard, a navigational light being out of service, or deteriorating weather.

sections.title: Repeating A MAYDAY Call After No Response
sections.text: If no acknowledgement is heard within about fifteen seconds of a MAYDAY call, repeat the full MAYDAY call unchanged: "MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, THIS IS SEA OTTER, SEA OTTER, SEA OTTER, MAYDAY SEA OTTER, POSITION FIVE ZERO DECIMAL ONE TWO NORTH, ZERO ZERO ONE DECIMAL FOUR FIVE WEST, TAKING ON WATER, FOUR PERSONS ON BOARD, REQUIRE IMMEDIATE ASSISTANCE, OVER." If there is still no answer after several repeated attempts, some DSC sets automatically retransmit the DSC distress alert; the operator should also try switching to Channel 70 briefly to confirm the DSC alert itself was sent, then return to Channel 16 to keep repeating the voice MAYDAY.

sections.title: Repeating Essential Information On MRCC Request
sections.text: When the MRCC (Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre) asks for a repeat of essential facts, respond promptly and slowly, digit by digit for anything numerical, and do not paraphrase: "THIS IS SEA OTTER, MY POSITION IS FIVE ZERO DEGREES ONE TWO DECIMAL FIVE MINUTES NORTH, ZERO ZERO ONE DEGREES FOUR FIVE DECIMAL THREE MINUTES WEST, PERSONS ON BOARD FIVE INCLUDING ONE INJURED, OVER."

sections.title: Responding To A Request For Continuous Situation Updates
sections.text:
When an MRCC requests continuous updates at defined intervals, acknowledge and follow a fixed schedule, for example every fifteen minutes on the working channel, and use a consistent structure each time: "MRCC, THIS IS SEA OTTER, UPDATE, POSITION FIVE ZERO DECIMAL ONE TWO NORTH ZERO ZERO ONE DECIMAL FOUR FIVE WEST, CONDITION NO CHANGE, NEXT UPDATE IN ONE FIVE MINUTES, OVER." If conditions worsen between scheduled updates, call immediately rather than waiting for the next scheduled slot.

A Full Escalation Sequence: Safety To Urgency To Medical Distress

A single developing situation can move through all three safety levels in sequence, and each stage needs its own correctly formatted call. First, a SECURITE warning is sent when a hazard is merely sighted: "SECURITE, SECURITE, SECURITE, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, HEAVY WEATHER DEVELOPING IN AREA, OUT." If the engine then fails and the vessel begins drifting seriously, this escalates to an urgency call: "PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, TOTAL LOSS OF PROPULSION, DRIFTING TOWARDS ROCKS, REQUESTING TOW, OVER." If a crew member is then injured and needs medical guidance, this becomes a PAN PAN MEDICO call, still using the PAN PAN urgency signal but specifically requesting medical advice rather than a general tow: "PAN PAN MEDICO, PAN PAN MEDICO, PAN PAN MEDICO, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, REQUESTING MEDICAL ADVICE FOR A CREW MEMBER WITH A SUSPECTED FRACTURE, OVER." If the vessel then genuinely starts taking on water and lives are in immediate danger, this escalates a final time to a full MAYDAY: "MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, TAKING ON WATER, FOUR PERSONS ON BOARD, REQUIRE IMMEDIATE ASSISTANCE, OVER." The key discipline is to always use the signal that matches the actual current severity of the situation, escalating (or de-escalating, once resolved) as conditions change, rather than jumping straight to MAYDAY for a situation that is not yet grave and imminent, or staying at a lower level once it genuinely becomes one.

When Not To Escalate Straight To MAYDAY

A vessel that is simply not under command, disabled, or requesting routine assistance is not automatically a MAYDAY situation; only grave and imminent danger to life justifies MAYDAY. For a vessel not under command but in no immediate danger, the correct call is a routine or, at most, a PAN PAN urgency call describing the situation and requesting assistance, not a distress call: "PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS SILENT WAVE, SILENT WAVE, SILENT WAVE, NOT UNDER COMMAND, DRIFTING, NO IMMEDIATE DANGER, REQUESTING A TOW, OVER." Sending an unwarranted MAYDAY diverts search-and-rescue resources from genuine emergencies and can result in the escalation being downgraded or disregarded by responding stations.

sections.title: De-Escalating Once A Situation Is Resolved
sections.text: Once the original danger has passed, whichever level was declared should be formally cancelled so other stations stop diverting attention or resources to it. For a resolved urgency situation: "ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, PAN PAN CANCEL, ASSISTANCE NO LONGER REQUIRED, OUT." For a resolved distress situation, the same pattern is used with MAYDAY: "ALL STATIONS, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, MAYDAY CANCEL, VESSEL SAFE, NO FURTHER ASSISTANCE REQUIRED, OUT."
